title: Episode 86: The Star-Spangled Banner at Fort McHenry: The Rocket's Red Glare of 1814
description:
The Star-Spangled Banner at Fort McHenry: The Rocket's Red Glare of 1814. How a twenty-five-hour British naval bombardment of Baltimore's harbor fortress failed to break American defenders, inspiring Francis Scott Key to write the words of the American national anthem. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into the War of 1812.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In September 1814, during the darkest hour of the War of 1812, the young United States faced imminent defeat. A battle-hardened British fleet had sailed up the Chesapeake Bay, burned Washington, D.C., incinerated the White House and the Capitol, and set its sights on Baltimore—a bustling maritime port that British admirals denounced as a 'nest of pirates.' Standing between the British fleet and the city was Fort McHenry, a star-shaped brick fortress manned by one thousand determined American soldiers and militia. Trapped aboard a truce vessel in the harbor, young Maryland lawyer Francis Scott Key watched an apocalyptic twenty-five-hour bombardment of over fifteen hundred explosive mortar bombs and Congreve rockets. When dawn broke through the smoke, the giant thirty-by-forty-two-foot banner was still waving. George brings us the thrilling story of the Star-Spangled Banner.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE BURNING OF THE CAPITAL AND THE MENACE ON BALTIMORE
In August eighteen fourteen, the War of 1812 reached a humiliating and desperate crisis for the United States. Following the defeat of Napoleon in Europe, Great Britain dispatched thousands of elite Wellington combat veterans and a powerful Royal Navy fleet to North America to punish the young republic. Sweeping into the Chesapeake Bay, British forces routed American militia at Bladensburg and marched unopposed into Washington, D.C., putting the torch to the White House, the Capitol, the Library of Congress, and the Navy Yard in a blaze of imperial vengeance. Flush with victory, British commanders Admiral Alexander Cochrane and Major General Robert Ross set their sights on their true strategic objective: the wealthy commercial boomtown of Baltimore, Maryland. Baltimore was the third-largest city in America and the premier hub of privateering schooners—fast, deadly raiders that had captured hundreds of British merchant vessels across the Atlantic. British leaders were determined to crush Baltimore, burn its shipyards, and plunder its merchant banks, bringing the American war effort to an absolute halt. British officers boasted that the Chesapeake Bay was now a British lake, openly predicting that Baltimore merchant houses would be plundered and burned to the ground before the winter gales closed the shipping lanes. President James Madison and his cabinet had fled Washington in confusion as British troops torched the executive mansion, leaving American morale shattered and the survival of the republic hanging in the balance.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: MAJOR ARMISTEAD AND THE GREAT GARRISON FLAG
Standing as the primary guardian of Baltimore's harbor entrance was Fort McHenry, a compact, star-shaped brick and earthen fortification situated on Whetstone Point, surrounded on three sides by the waters of the Patapsco River. Command of the fort fell to Major George Armistead, a resolute, thirty-four-year-old Virginia artilleryman who understood the immense historical stakes. Armistead commanded a garrison of approximately one thousand men: regular army artillerists, volunteer Baltimore city militia, sailors from the Chesapeake Flotilla under Commodore Joshua Barney, and free Black volunteers. Anticipating the British assault, Armistead declared that the fort needed a flag 'so large that the British will have no difficulty seeing it from a distance.' Major Armistead commissioned Baltimore flagmaker Mary Pickersgill to sew a colossal garrison banner measuring thirty feet wide and forty-two feet long, featuring fifteen broad red and white stripes and fifteen giant two-foot stars stitched from four hundred yards of English wool bunting. Armistead also sank two dozen merchant sailing hulls in the narrow channel before the fort, creating an impassable underwater reef that prevented British warships from entering the inner harbor. Mary Pickersgill and her daughters worked by candlelight in a Baltimore brewery malt house to stitch the enormous garrison flag, piecing together fifteen woolen stripes two feet wide so it would wave proudly above the Patapsco. Major Armistead ordered the sunken hulls in the ship channel packed with stone ballast, creating an impassable barrier that prevented British frigates from bringing their heavy broadsides within point-blank range of the fort.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: FRANCIS SCOTT KEY AND THE TRUCE VESSEL
As the British fleet approached Baltimore, an unexpected legal mission pulled thirty-five-year-old Georgetown lawyer and amateur poet Francis Scott Key into the center of the conflict. Following the burning of Washington, British troops had arrested an elderly, respected Maryland physician named Dr. William Beanes on dubious charges of detaining British stragglers. Accompanied by the United States Prisoner Exchange Agent John S. Skinner, Key boarded the British flagship HMS Tonnant under a formal flag of truce to negotiate Dr. Beanes's release. Key presented letters written by wounded British soldiers who testified that Dr. Beanes had treated their combat wounds with exemplary medical kindness. Impressed by the evidence, British Admiral Cochrane agreed to release the physician. However, because Key and Skinner had overheard operational planning and military secrets regarding the imminent combined naval and land attack on Baltimore, Cochrane informed them that they could not return to shore until the battle was over. Key was placed under armed guard aboard the truce sloop Minden, anchored four miles downstream with a direct, unobstructed view of Fort McHenry's star ramparts. Key and Skinner were escorted aboard the British flagship under armed guard, where they presented official letters from wounded British prisoners testifying to the humane medical care provided by Dr. William Beanes. Key was forced to remain aboard the truce vessel as the British war council finalized plans to bombard Fort McHenry, listening helplessly as British officers wagered on how many hours the American fortress would survive.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE INFERNO OF THE BOMB VESSELS
At six thirty on the rainy morning of Tuesday, September thirteenth, eighteen fourteen, the British naval assault began with catastrophic fury. Admiral Cochrane deployed five specialized heavy bomb vessels—the Meteor, Volcano, Aetna, Terror, and Devastation—anchored two miles from Fort McHenry, just outside the range of the fort's smaller thirty-six-pounder smoothbore cannon. For twenty-five continuous hours, British bomb ships fired massive cast-iron mortar shells weighing two hundred and twenty pounds each, packed with gunpowder and fitted with timed powder fuses designed to detonate in mid-air over the defenders' heads or plunge through brick bombproofs. Simultaneously, the specialized rocket ship HMS Erebus unleashed hundreds of Congreve rockets—thirty-two-pound incendiary rockets with sixteen-foot guide sticks that screamed across the water, trailing roaring streams of sparks and exploding in terrifying showers of red flame and shrapnel. Major Armistead's artillerists could only huddle beneath earthen parapets as over fifteen hundred mortar bombs and rockets rained down upon the fort in an apocalyptic torrent. The concussive shockwaves of the exploding mortar bombs rattled windowpanes in Baltimore five miles away, while sulfurous smoke drifted across the harbor, plunging the bay into a terrifying artificial twilight. The Congreve rockets fired by HMS Erebus created terrifying screaming sounds as their propellant ignited, trailing long tails of sparks across the rainy night sky and exploding with deafening concussive bursts above the bastions.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE MIDNIGHT CRISIS AND THE SNEAK ATTACK
At two o'clock on the rainy afternoon of September thirteenth, a British mortar shell scored a direct hit on the southwest bastion, crashing directly into Fort McHenry's primary powder magazine, which contained three hundred barrels of gunpowder. In an astonishing stroke of providence, the shell's fuse sputtered and failed to ignite the powder, sparing the garrison from total annihilation. Armistead immediately ordered the powder distributed in small caches behind earthen ramparts. Seeing the fort's guns fall silent to conserve ammunition, British commanders mistakenly believed the defenders were broken. Shortly after midnight on September fourteenth, under cover of heavy rain and pitch darkness, British Captain Charles Napier launched a daring amphibious flanking raid: twenty barges carrying twelve hundred elite British soldiers and sailors rowed silently past the fort, intending to land behind American lines and storm the city. But American gunners at secondary shoreline batteries—Fort Covington and the Babcock battery—spotted the reflection of oars in the lightning. The batteries opened up with a devastating crossfire of grapeshot and canister, sinking several barges and forcing the British raiders to retreat with heavy casualties, crushing the final British hope of seizing the harbor. American artillerists held their fire with iron discipline, waiting until the British raiding barges were illuminated by rocket glare before opening a murderous crossfire of grapeshot that broke the flanking attack. The dud mortar shell that pierced the powder magazine was viewed by the defenders as a direct act of divine providence, reinforcing Major Armistead determination to hold the fort at all costs.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE DAWN'S EARLY LIGHT
Out in the harbor aboard the Minden, Francis Scott Key spent the agonizing night pacing the deck in torrential rain, watching the crimson glare of exploding rockets illuminate the darkness and listening to the concussive roar of mortar shells that shook the water beneath the hull. Shortly after three o'clock in the morning, the British bombardment suddenly ceased: a heavy, eerie silence settled over the misty bay. Key knew that the silence could mean only one of two things: either the British had abandoned the attack, or Fort McHenry had surrendered and struck its colors. Key strained his eyes through the morning fog, praying for the first light of dawn. At six o'clock on Wednesday morning, September fourteenth, a gentle breeze parted the lingering sulfurous smoke and sea mist. As the morning sun broke over the water, Key raised his spyglass to the fort's ninety-foot flagpole. There, waving proudly above the star ramparts, was not the British Union Jack, but Mary Pickersgill's colossal fifteen-stripe Star-Spangled Banner, gently rippling in the morning wind. The fort had held. Baltimore was saved. The British fleet was in full retreat. Through his brass spyglass, Francis Scott Key watched the crimson glow of burning rockets fade as dawn approached, his heart pounding in suspense as the morning breeze slowly parted the heavy veil of harbor mist. When Key saw the giant wool flag rippling in the morning breeze above the ramparts, tears of joy filled his eyes, knowing that Baltimore was saved and that American freedom had survived the British empire greatest assault.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE ANTHEM OF A FREE PEOPLE
Overwhelmed by relief and patriotic joy, Francis Scott Key pulled an old letter from his pocket and began scribbling lines of poetry on the back of the envelope, immortalizing the dramatic scene he had just witnessed: 'O say can you see by the dawn's early light, what so proudly we hailed at the twilight's last gleaming.' Arriving in Baltimore following his release, Key completed the four stanzas in his hotel room at the Indian Queen Tavern. Entitled 'The Defence of Fort M'Henry,' the poem was printed as a handbill by the Baltimore American newspaper and set to the popular tune of an old English melody, 'To Anacreon in Heaven.' Within weeks, the song was sung in theatres, taverns, and military camps across the nation, retitled 'The Star-Spangled Banner.' In nineteen thirty-one, Congress officially declared Key's composition the national anthem of the United States. Today, Mary Pickersgill's original garrison flag is preserved in a permanent climate-controlled sanctuary at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C., its scorched wool fibers and missing star an eternal testament to the defenders of Fort McHenry who proved that liberty would endure through the darkest night. The poem was hastily printed on handbills and distributed throughout Baltimore under the title The Defence of Fort MHenry, set to an old English melody and sung by crowds celebrating their deliverance from British tyranny. Key poetic verses captured the emotional soul of a young nation, transforming the sight of a battle-torn flag into a universal symbol of freedom, resilience, and democratic hope that endures across generations.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Star-Spangled Banner at Fort McHenry proved that courage under fire could forge an enduring national identity. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we journey to the Eastern Shore of Maryland for the legendary exploits of Harriet Tubman and the Underground Railroad.
